segments.say: Lesson 11. A P I Design: rest, GraphQL, G R P C & Real-time. Resource design, idempotency keys, pagination, versioning, plus polling versus long-polling versus S S E versus WebSockets.

A P I design is deciding the endpoints, data formats and rules clients use to talk to your service, so they're clear, safe to retry, efficient, and able to evolve. Here is an analogy. Designing a restaurant menu: clear item names, prices, what happens if you order twice by accident, and how to add new dishes without confusing regulars.

Why does this matter? The "A P I" step appears in every design answer. Real-time choices (WebSockets versus S S E) come up in chat and notification designs. A few key words. rest: Resource U R Ls plus H T T P methods. GraphQL: Client asks for exactly the fields it needs. G R P C: Fast binary service-to-service calls. Idempotency: Repeating a request has no extra effect. Pagination: Returning results page by page.

segments.say: Same key leads to A P I returns the saved response without charging again. Retries become safe. Stripe and every payment A P I work this way.
Real-time options. Short polling: "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple, but lots of empty responses and delayed updates.
Long polling: the server holds the request open until there's data (or timeout), then the client immediately re-asks. Near real-time over plain H T T P.
S S E: one H T T P connection, the server pushes a stream of events. Perfect for one-way feeds such as notifications, live scores and L L M token streaming.
WebSocket: a persistent two-way connection. Chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing. Needs stateful connection servers and sticky routing.

rest design checklist. Nouns for resources: G E T /users/42/orders, P O S T /orders. Correct verbs and status codes. G E T, P U T, DELETE are idempotent; P O S T isn't, unless you add an idempotency key. Pagination: cursor-based (?after=abc&limit=20 ) is stable and fast for feeds; offset (?page=3 ) is simple but slow and shifts on inserts. Versioning: /v1/ in the path or a header. Never break clients silently. Filtering, sorting, consistent error format, rate-limit headers, auth (OAuth2 / J W T).

When to use which. rest: public A P Is, C R U D, cacheable over H T T P. GraphQL: many clients needing different shapes of nested data in one round trip. Watch N+1 queries and caching complexity. G R P C: internal service-to-service: Protobuf binary, H T T P/2, streaming, strict contracts. Fast.

Say it in the interview. "Public A P I: rest with resource-oriented U R Ls, cursor pagination, versioning and idempotency keys on P O S Ts that move money or create orders. Internally, G R P C for low-latency typed calls. For live updates, S S E when it's server-to-client only, WebSockets when it's bidirectional, like chat.".

Let's compare. Format: jason over H T T P, jason, single endpoint, Protobuf over H T T P/2. Strength: simple, cacheable, universal, client picks fields, no over-fetch, fast, typed, streaming. Weakness: over/under-fetching, caching, N+1, complexity, browser support, debugging. Use: public A P Is, mobile/web B F Fs, internal microservices.

Real-time. Short polling: client pulls, new request each time, rare updates, simplicity. Long polling: client pulls (held), held open, fallback real-time. S S E: server leads to client, one long H T T P stream, notifications, L L M streaming. WebSocket: both ways, persistent T C P, chat, games, collaboration.

A likely interview question: How do you design an A P I for payments? A strong answer: rest resources, P O S T /payments with a required Idempotency-Key, proper status codes, auth, rate limits, versioning, webhooks for async status, and cursor pagination for listings.
That's it for A P I Design: rest, GraphQL, G R P C & Real-time. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
